'''Ibrahim ibn Sinan''' ([[Arabic]]: ''Ibrāhīm ibn Sinān ibn Thābit ibn Qurra'', {{Lang|ar|ابراهيم بن سنان بن ثابت بن قرة}}; born 295{{snd}}296 AH/{{circa|908}} in [[Baghdad]], died: 334-335 AH/946 in Baghdad, aged 38) was a [[mathematician]] and [[astronomer]] who belonged to a family of scholars originally from [[Harran]] in northern [[Mesopotamia]]. He was the son of [[Sinan ibn Thabit]] ({{circa|880}}{{snd}}943) and the grandson of [[Thābit ibn Qurra]] ({{circa|830}}{{snd}}901).{{sfn|Van Brummelen|2007|p=574}} Like his grandfather, he belonged to a religious sect of [[star worship]]pers known as the [[Sabians of Harran]].<ref>{{harvnb|Roberts|2017|p=253}}.</ref>

Ibrahim ibn Sinan studied [[geometry]], in particular [[tangents]] to circles. He made advances in the [[Quadrature (geometry)|quadrature]] of the [[parabola]] and the theory of [[Integral|integration]], generalizing the work of [[Archimedes]], which was unavailable at the time.{{sfn|Van Brummelen|2007|p=574}}<ref name="mactutor" /> Ibrahim ibn Sinan is often considered to be one of the most important mathematicians of his time.<ref name="mactutor">{{MacTutor|id=Ibrahim|title=Ibrahim ibn Sinan ibn Thabit ibn Qurra}}</ref>
